News.title: Granada earthquake - live: Building collapses as 4.8-magnitude tremor rocks Spain
News.content:
An earthquake measuring 4.8 on the Richter scale has shaken the holiday hotspot of Granada in Spain.

A powerful earthquake has shaken the Spanish city of Granada, spreading panic and causing a building to collapse.

The tremor, which was also felt in neighbouring provinces such as Almeria, has registered as a 4.8 on the Richter scale. It comes following an earthquake on Saturday that measured 5 and left a trail of destruction with panicking holidaymakers running from their hotels.

The southern city of Granada, known for its stunning Alhambra Palace, was rocked by the latest tremor just after 10.30am local time. Residents felt the walls and ceilings shake with footage showing one building crumbling into the street.

News.title: Meta child safety trial could have 'astronomical' global impact for Facebook and Instagram
News.content:
The impact on Facebook and Instagram could be "astronomical" should Meta lose a high-stakes trial regarding the safety and privacy of children on its social media platforms.

Meta, the parent company behind Facebook, Instagram and others, faces a major lawsuit today in a federal court in Oakland, California, that could lead to critical changes for the social media juggernaut. A coalition of 29 US states brought a single case against Meta alleging the company violated numerous federal and state child privacy laws - the company strongly denies the allegations.

The states, including California and New York, claim Meta contributed to a mental health crisis among children and had deliberately created design features that keep youngsters addicted to social media. It also alleges Meta gathers data from children aged 13 without the consent of their parents, a major breach of US federal law if proven accurate.

View 9 Images Mark Zuckerberg's Meta faces a major lawsuit that could change the company's future (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Teenagers face block on overnight access and addictive social media features READ MORE :

Terrifying rogue AI bots spark fears humanity is losing control READ MORE :

"This week, we’re in court with the largest consumer protection lawsuit in American history," said Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman in a statement. "We’ll show a jury that Meta concealed what it knew about the harm its products cause young people because looking away was more profitable."

The move has been compared to the humbling of US tobacco corporations in 1998, which forced major changes to marketing cigarettes and other products as well as companies agreeing to pay US states for medical expenses related to smoking. "AGs are in the perfect position to get this done," Coleman said. "We did it with the Tobacco Settlement in the 1990s. We did it with the companies behind the opioid crisis. We’ll do it again with Meta."

What allegations does Meta face?

View 9 Images A majority of US adults said they have used Facebook (Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

The lawsuit alleges Meta illegally collected and used data of children aged under 13 who were using its social media platforms. It also claimed the company made decisions in designing its platforms that drove excessive use "and put young users at risk, and lied to users, their families, and the public about the safety of its platforms."

The US Attorney Generals allege Meta violated federal and state laws, including the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) as well as the New Jersey Consumer Protection Act. COPPA, introduced in 1998, many years before Meta's founding, requires websites, apps as well as other online services to gain verified parental consent before collecting data from children aged under 13.

The lawsuit, originally filed in 2023, also claims "harmful" features on Instagram and Facebook drove excessive use by children and teenagers that caused them to be distracted at school and disrupted their ability to sleep at night, "all the while misleading users, their families, and the public about the existence and severity of these risks."

'Astronomical' consequences

View 9 Images Mark Zuckerberg would be ordered to make changes at Meta should his company lose the lawsuit (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Meta lost a similar case in New Mexico and will be forced to make services to its online services as well as pay the equivalent of £855,555,000. Should Meta lose the lawsuit, the consequences could be far more stark for the company.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez told the CNBC following the victory in his state that the consequences would be "astronomical" for the company that generates some 98 per cent of its revenue from online advertising. He added: "This is a state with some 2 million people. If you map that same argument onto California or Florida or Texas or New York, I mean, that’s a potentially massive and a market shifting force."

California holds enormous influence and could impose harsher penalties, which includes a major overhaul of how algorithms are implemented. "California matters more than any other jurisdiction in the US," Julia Powles, executive director of the UCLA Institute for Technology, Law and Policy told CNBC. "It’s where they are subject to the greatest legal reach, and it’s a jurisdiction watched around the world."

What could ruling mean for UK?

View 9 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham could follow the ruling closely (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Should Meta lose the lawsuit in California, it would not only have implications across the US but will likely extend to the UK as well. The decision would likely "shape ongoing global debates about the extraordinary power and influence wielded by social media companies over infrastructure, behaviour and norms that shape the lives of social media users, and how to ensure that social media companies are held accountable," said Dr Hellen Mukiri-Smith from Loughborough University's Department of Law.

She noted while there had been efforts to regulate social media such as the UK's Online Safety Act, regulatory challenges remain. It remains unclear whether politicians and regulators would take steps to regulate the design of social media that protects rights.

Following the New Mexico ruling, ex-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said his government would" study the ruling very carefully." He added the government would trial social media bans and digital curfews in the homes of 300 teens in the UK.

Majority of Americans want tougher social media rules

View 9 Images Many Americans want restrictions on social media companies (Image: Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

Facebook, Instagram and YouTube were the most popular online platforms, according to a November 2025 Pew Research survey. It found 84 per cent of US adults said they had used YouTube, 71 per cent report using Facebook and 50 per cent had accessed Instagram.

Smaller numbers use TikTok (37 per cent) and WhatsApp (32 per cent). It also noted fewer used Reddit (26 per cent), Snapchat (25 per cent) and X/Twitter (21 per cent).

A Reuters/Ipsos survey of US adults carried out earlier this month found 61 per cent of respondents believed social media firms should face tighter regulation. Some 66 per cent also supported using age-verification to prevent children 16 from accessing social media sites.

Social media 'public nuisance'

View 9 Images Social media companies were branded a "public nuisance" by a New Mexico judge (Image: VCG via Getty Images)

Judge Bryan Biedscheid branded Meta a "public nuisance" following the New Mexico verdict. His order includes banning Instagram and Facebook from counting likes for users under 18. It also bans teens from sending or receiving nude images via the platforms.

He added Meta was like a factory that was polluting the air that people breathe and caused "harmful effects" that had impacts on the entire population.

Judge Biedscheid's order only applies to New Mexico. Should the lawsuit brought by dozens of state emerge victorious, it could lead to sweeping changes across the entire US.

Meta's previous lawsuit loss

View 9 Images Mark Zuckerberg was present during the previous lawsuit (Image: Getty Images)

Mark Zuckerberg's Meta has suffered previous losses amid as more people continue demand tougher social media rules. Earlier this year, a Los Angeles jury handed down a legal defeat against Meta and YouTube over a young woman's childhood addiction to online platforms.

The woman, known only as Kaley, was awarded £4.5 million in damages, after a jury found Meta and Google, which owns YouTube, deliberately built addictive platforms that damaged the 20-year-old's mental health. Meta and Google said they would appeal the verdict.

Meta's response

View 9 Images Meta has denied the allegations against it (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Meta has strongly denied the allegations in the lawsuit. The company attempted to dismiss the coalition lawsuit in 2024 - an effort which was blocked and in June this year a court fully denied its attempt to terminate the lawsuit.

"These lawsuits misportray our company and the work we do every day to provide young people with safe, valuable experiences online," Meta said in a previous statement. "Striking a balance between allowing teens to access the benefits of social media while keeping them safe is one of the most critical questions across our industry.

"We have listened to parents, researched the issues that matter most, and made real changes to protect teens online – like introducing Teen Accounts with built-in protections and providing parents with tools to manage their teens’ experiences.

"Despite the snippets of conversations or cherry-picked quotes that plaintiffs’ counsel may use to paint an intentionally misleading picture of the company, we’re proud of the progress we’ve made, we stand by our record of putting teen safety first, and we’ll keep making improvements."

News.title: Man stops at traffic light then spots familiar face sitting in car next to him
News.content:
Man stops at traffic light then spots familiar face sitting in car next to him

Stopping at a red light can turn into a frustratingly long wait, but for one man he couldn't quite believe his eyes when he looked to see who was sat in the car metres away from him

View Image You never know who you might bump into at the traffic light (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Being stuck at a traffic light is no fun, but it's a good chance to catch a breather if you've been at the wheel for a while. It's not always common to spot a familiar face metres away from you, but one man recently had that happen to him.

‌



After landing in New York, US, the bloke decided to go for a drive around the Big Apple when he stopped at a red light signal. He decided to have a glance at the car sitting on his left, only to be left surprised it was someone he'd recognise. Now in a clip shared on social media, the man claimed he saw American actor and comedian Tracy Morgan.

‌



In the TikTok video, he said: "First thing I see in NYC... Tracy Morgan." The quick shot shows a driver sitting in a red Lamborghini Aventador SVJ Roadster with his roof top down.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

While the user is convinced it was the star, previous sightings of Morgan in his Lambo seem to suggest it could well have been him. The comedian, originally from Brooklyn, has been spotted on numerous occasions cruising around in his beloved sportscar.

Previous Reddit posts have also captured the film star in his Lambo, driving down iconic New York streets like Times Square and Manhattan neighbourhood Washington Heights.

‌



In recent months, Morgan has also been spotted cheering on the Knicks where he "cried like a baby" as they clinched their first NBA title in 53 years, beating San Antonio Spurs in Game 5.

And since the 30 Rock star is very much living his best life in New York, it's quite normal for locals to spot him around the area. One wrote on Reddit: "I live up here too. I've seen him and gotten a wave from him before."

Another added: "Tracy has a reputation in NY as a Certified Good Dude."

‌



What is Tracy Morgan up to nowadays?

Morgan is stars in the comedy series The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins, which first aired on NBC this year. He plays a former professional athlete trying to document his epic comeback to football.

Last year, he starred as Harlem shop owner Frank "Crutch" Crutchfield in this Paramount+ comedy series, which served as a spinoff to The Neighborhood.

Article continues below

He's believed to be playing in theatre and casino venues across the US for his stand-up comedy tours.

In other life updates, Morgan revealed he'd fed 19,000 families through his charity work, where he told PEOPLE it was "one of the greatest joys" in his life.

He also opened up about his near-fatal crash in 2024 with Oprah Winfrey, which left him with severe traumatic brain injuries and broken bones.

News.title: First pictures of Brit man and wife dead in helicopter crash on Greece honeymoon
News.content:
First pictures of Brit man and wife dead in helicopter crash on Greece honeymoon

Newlyweds Alex Cromie and Marie Ebert tragically died in a helicopter crash in Sifnos, Greece, on Monday with the company Alex worked for, Blackstone, saying he was 'beloved by everyone'

View Image Alexander Cromie and Marie Ebert have been killed in a helicopter crash while on holiday (Image: Facebook)

A British man and his wife who died in a helicopter crash while celebrating their honeymoon have been pictured for the first time.

‌



Alex Cromie and Marie Ebert, in their early 30s, died alongside helicopter pilot Giorgos Raikos after the chopper span out of control on a journey from Athens to the island of Sifnos.

‌



In a statement issued by asset management firm Blackstone, where Mr Cromie worked as a vice president in private wealth solutions, a spokesperson said: “We are shocked by the tragic passing of three people including our colleague Alex Cromie and his wife Marie Ebert, who were celebrating their honeymoon.

‌



“Alex was beloved by everyone who knew and worked with him at Blackstone, and our thoughts and prayers are with his loved ones.”

Raikos, 55, was described in local reports as an experienced former Greek Air Force officer who had flown military Chinook helicopters.

‌



The helicopter crashed and sparked a fire in the Tholos part of Sifnos with residents living close to the helipad reported hearing an unusual noise from the aircraft shortly before the crash.

Manolis Fountoulakis, deputy mayor of Sifnos, told ERTnews: "According to the testimonies of the residents of the area, they heard the noise of the helicopter, it was a strange noise.

"It probably had a mechanical failure in the air. This is because the propeller was doing something strange… it was making a very loud noise."

Article continues below

Fountoulakis said residents had described hearing a noise "like military aircraft" before the helicopter came down. Authorities are reconstructing the helicopter's flight path and analysing footage of the crash as part of their investigation.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office has been contacted for comment.

News.title: King officially starts Balmoral holiday amid claims disgraced Andrew ‘rejected’ offer to stay
News.content:
King officially starts Balmoral holiday amid claims disgraced Andrew ‘rejected’ offer to stay

King Charles has been given a formal ceremonial welcome at Balmoral today as he officially starts his holiday there and will welcome family members to stay over the coming weeks

View 5 Images The King officially taking up residence at Balmoral today (Image: Jane Barlow/PA Wire Picture date: Tuesday August 18, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Jane Barlow/PA Wire)

The King has officially started his Balmoral holiday with a ceremonial welcome outside the castle.

Charles has carried on with the tradition of his late mother by holding a ceremony to mark his official stay in residence at the Scottish Highlands estate.

Dressed in his traditional kilt, the monarch inspected a Guard of Honour formed by the Balaklava Company, 5th Battalion the Royal Regiment of Scotland.

Troops also played the pipes and drums at the ceremony, with the regiment's mascot - a tiny Shetland pony called Corporal Cruachan IV - also there.

During his stay at Balmoral for the rest of the summer, the King is expected to welcome up to 30 family members, who travel to Scotland to spend time with him at the estate.

Should Prince Harry visit the UK more often? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

King Charles opens historic part of Sandringham estate for overnight stays for first time READ MORE :

View 5 Images The King with his younger brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, last year (Image: AP)

Among them are the Prince and Princess of Wales and their three children - Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis. However, one family member not expected to travel to Balmoral this year is the King’s shamed brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, after claims by friends of the ex-prince that he was offered the chance of a holiday there but turned it down.

A pal of the former Duke of York alleges he rejected the invitation as he feared he would be treated like an ‘outcast’ if he travelled there.

It is believed that his older brother Charles, who stripped Mr Mountbatten-Windsor of his royal titles and booted him out of his Royal Lodge mansion, has not seen him this year, despite the two only being a mile apart when the monarch stays at Sandringham.

View 5 Images King Charles greets Shetland pony Corporal Cruachan IV during the Balmoral ceremony (Image: Jane Barlow/PA Wire Picture date: Tuesday August 18, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Jane Barlow/PA Wire)

It is thought only Prince Edward has seen him since he was arrested on his 66th birthday and moved to Marsh Farm, following new claims about his association with paedophile Jeffrey Epstein. He was last seen publicly with members of the Firm at the funeral of the Duchess of Kent last September. He denies all wrongdoing.

A friend of Mr Mountbatten-Windsor's told The Sun: "Andrew feels he’s been abandoned. He feels like he is no longer part of the family.

"He was invited but has got no great desire to be at Balmoral as he has nothing to gain and would be treated as an outcast. What’s the point, he feels, of going all the way there for a much-needed holiday and being treated as an elephant in the room?"

View 5 Images The King carries out an inspection of the Balaklava Company, 5th Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland (Image: Jane Barlow/PA Wire Picture date: Tuesday August 18, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Jane Barlow/PA Wire)

It comes as the King has been in Scotland for several weeks already this month, enjoying his annual stay at the Castle of Mey, once beloved by his grandmother, the Queen Mother.

During his time there, he has also attended the Castle of Mey Games, met the Assynt Mountain Rescue team, visited the communities of Halkirk and Castletown, and opened a distillery housed in a restored former mill building.

Meanwhile, during today’s ceremony, the King also welcomed the first two members of the Balmoral Highlander, which Charles has revived following their disbandment in 1936 under George V. Both the new Highlanders are employees of the Balmoral Estate and will also take part in the Braemar Gathering in September.

View 5 Images Charles waves as he goes through the castle gates (Image: Jane Barlow/PA Wire Picture date: Tuesday August 18, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Jane Barlow/PA Wire)

In keeping with tradition, each Highlander carries a ceremonial Lochaber Axe and wears a Highland uniform which takes inspiration from the original uniform worn in the late 1800s.

The kilt and plaid are made from the Balmoral Glen Gelder tartan which was designed by The Scottish Tartans Authority at the request of the King.

Article continues below

The Mirror has contacted Buckingham Palace for comment.

News.title: British couple on honeymoon killed in helicopter crash on Greek island
News.content:
A young British couple and their pilot were killed in a helicopter crash on the Greek island of Sifnos on Monday, Greek police have said.

They have been named as newlyweds Alexander Cromie and Marie Ebert, who were in Greece on their honeymoon.

The private helicopter crashed just metres from a landing pad, killing the pair and their pilot, a Greek national.

The couple are said to have taken the helicopter from the village of Markopoulo near Athens to the popular holiday island, Kathimerini reported.

Greece's aviation safety authority told the BBC it was investigating the crash and that its investigators were heading to the scene on Tuesday to gather evidence and speak to witnesses.

News.title: Young adults are taking prescription drugs instead of alcohol - and it's dividing experts
News.content:
To enjoy a night out with friends, Matt once had to drink until he felt sick.

If he didn't, the 22-year-old from the north of England would spend the night silent, terrified of saying the wrong thing. The warehouse worker says it felt like there was "just no way into" the conversations everyone else seemed to be enjoying.

Then, two years ago, he swapped pints for prescription drugs he discovered through social media.

As he gets ready to go out on a Friday, Matt, whose name has been changed, now takes a medicine he purchases illegally online that usually treats epilepsy and nerve pain; alongside a beta blocker designed to slow a racing heart and relax trembling muscles (physical symptoms of anxiety).

He says it gives him the effects of alcohol without the hangover.

"The amount of alcohol you have to drink to replicate the effects of these is really unhealthy and it doesn't feel good," he says. Matt says the drugs he takes leave him feeling "euphoric," quietens his anxious thoughts and makes socialising easy, he says.

But experts say taking the drugs without medical supervision at high doses can be dangerous and, in some cases, life-threatening. Long-term use of the drugs can also result in dependency; users find they rely on it for any social situation. They also report increased anxiety, insomnia, and suicidal thoughts when they try to come off the drug.

News.title: Serco employee charged with misconduct over sharing asylum seeker addresses
News.content:
An employee of a company that provides accommodation for asylum seekers has been charged with misconduct in public office over sharing the properties' addresses.

Houses in St John's Way, Bracken Road, Clover Way, Elm Road and Chester Way in Thetford, Norfolk, were targeted by crowds over three nights earlier this month.

James Jobson, 62, from Highlow Road, Costessey, near Norwich, works at Serco and appeared at Ipswich Magistrates' Court on Monday.

He was remanded in custody and will appear at Norwich Crown Court on 14 September.

The charge stated that between 3 and 14 August, while acting as a public officer employed by Serco, Jobson "wilfully and without reasonable excuse or justification" committed misconduct in a way which "amounted to an abuse of the public's trust in the office".

Norfolk Police said the charge was in connection to the "release of information relating to a number of addresses in Thetford, which were later targeted during several nights of violent disorder in the town".

A spokesperson for Serco said: "This matter is currently being handled by the police, and we are cooperating fully. As this relates to an ongoing legal process, it would be inappropriate to comment further."

News.title: Heavy showers and thunderstorms bring risk of flash flooding to UK
News.content:
Wet weather is forecast for parts of the UK following a summer of record-breaking heatwaves and widespread drought.

Although heavy showers are expected for many, the places across England and Wales most in need of significant rain may not see much of it in the coming days.

Most of the showers will fall across parts of north-west England, Northern Ireland and southern Scotland, with some parts of south-east England staying dry.

Where the heaviest showers do fall, there is a risk of hail, lightning and the potential for flash flooding.

News.title: Burnham says he's not embarrassed about hoax message exchange
News.content:
Andy Burnham says he is not embarrassed that he exchanged messages with a person posing as US President Donald Trump's chief of staff.

The prime minister added all politicians face "these challenges" but insisted he did "everything right" in how he handled the security breach.

News website Politico first reported, external that Burnham communicated with a person claiming to be Susie Wiles. Burnham said there was a "minimal exchange of information of zero consequence".

Liberal Democrat MP James MacCleary has written to Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC) to ask them to consider investigating what he called an "egregious security breach".

It is understood the communication between Burnham and the person posing as Wiles was in the form of messages and there was no conversation between the two.

Asked if he was embarrassed about the incident, Burnham told broadcasters: "No, I am not because there was a minimal exchange, nothing of consequence and quickly I realised that this needed to be reported and I did so.

"So I handled it in the right way. All politicians are receiving these pressures and these challenges, but I did everything right."

Pressed on what action is being taken to find out who was behind the incident and to improve systems, Burnham said the "correct action" had been taken both in the UK and the US, without providing further details.

MacCleary, in his letter to ISC chairman Lord Beamish, said the security of the prime minister's communications "ought to be an absolute priority".

He added: "We need to understand how this breach could occur, or else risk it being repeated."

News.title: OpenAI makes ChatGPT less 'human' for teens in new safety update
News.content:
The maker of ChatGPT is rolling out a range of new safety features today for under-18s who use the AI chatbot.

Those with new teen accounts will be able to switch off the human voice response, in order to minimise the tech's ability to appear like a person.

OpenAI is also introducing regular reminders for young people to take a break from using the tool, reminding them ChatGPT is AI, and saying "it can wait".

The firm insisted this was not in response to a particular issue with children believing ChatGPT to be alive - but there are growing concerns about people becoming convinced that the AI tools they interact with are sentient.

Last year Mustafa Suleyman, the head of AI at rival firm Microsoft, said "seemingly conscious" AI products "kept him awake at night" because he was so worried about their impact on society.

In other areas, OpenAI seems to be loosely following the teen account model developed by the large social networks.

In a blog post announcing ChatGPT for Teens, external, the firm said teenagers' use of AI "should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time".

It said teen accounts would become the default for those who identified themselves as teenagers when they signed up, and others whom the firm itself identified as under 18.

But it did not elaborate on how it would identify these teens.

Under-13s are not allowed to use the product.

News.title: Officers told not to pursue car on wrong side of motorway before crash, says Ireland's police body
News.content:
GardaÃ­ (Irish police) were instructed to disengage from pursuing a car as it drove in the wrong direction on a motorway before a fatal crash, the Garda Representative Association has said.

Five teenagers were killed in the head-on crash on the M9 in County Kildare on Sunday morning.

Two women are in a critical condition, while another woman and a seven-year-old boy are in a serious condition.

Assistant General Secretary of the Garda Representative Association (GRA), Tara McManus, told the BBC that garda roads policing officers "do not have pursuit training".

She said officers involved in the Kildare incident were given a command to "disengage" with the car after it took "evasive action".

Ireland's Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan said that the Garda Commissioner has said he would introduce pursuit training this year.

The crash happened on the M9 Northbound at Junction 3 at about 03:00 local time.

The five teenagers who died have been named locally as Joe Carthy from Athy, County Kildare, Alex McCarthy from Carlow, Kamil Pustkowski from Limerick, Jeremy O'Brien and Jack Kennedy, according to Irish broadcaster RTÃ News.

The injured family - two women aged in their 30s and one in her 20s, and the young boy - are understood to be from Carlow.

McManus said the teenagers had been in the car for a number of hours before the collision and gardaÃ­ had attempted to interact with them and bring the vehicle to a stop on "several occasions".

She told BBC NI's Good Morning Ulster programme that officers deployed stinger devices in an attempt to stop the car, but it proceeded to travel in the direction of the motorway.

"At that stage our members would not continue in that pursuit and the directions that were given by our command and control centre were to disengage," she said.

"That would be the normal procedure for us that we do not engage with a car that has decided to take that sort of evasive action."

News.title: Wetherspoons bans customers playing music from phones in pubs
News.content:
Wetherspoons has banned its customers from playing music out loud or taking calls on speaker, saying the noise from phones and tablets was an increasing problem driving people "nuts".

The company â which runs 792 pubs and bars across the UK â said that following complaints it has asked customers to switch their devices to silent or to use earphones.

Polling in recent years by various organisations suggests people are largely opposed to others playing music or taking calls on speaker in public spaces.

Wetherspoons told the BBC that staff would be asked to use "common sense" when enforcing the ban.

"We are not looking to ask anyone to leave a pub if they go against the ruling, but it is an option for managers if they refuse to do so," the company said.

The British Beer and Pub Association, which represents Wetherspoons and several other pub companies in the UK, said that "having a clear policy helps staff enforce rules and customers know what they can and can't do".

The group added: "We're yet to hear of anyone who relishes having a pint against the backdrop of a speakerphone call or someone loudly playing a video, so we expect this move will be greatly welcomed."

Studies suggest the majority of Britons are annoyed by hearing people take calls on speakerphone or playing videos or music on their phones without headphones.

A Transport for London survey of 1,000 people last year found 70% of respondents found loud music and phone calls without headphones a nuisance.

However, the evidence also suggests there is a clear generational gap. In an Ofcom survey of 1,010 people in August 2022, of the 13-to-17-year-olds questioned, 69% said it was acceptable to make video calls, 73% to listen to music and 83% to watch videos without headphones.

News.title: Scotland's state-owned shipyard to cut a quarter of its workforce
News.content:
Scotland's state-owned shipyard is to cut nearly a quarter of its total workforce while it waits for confirmation of promised new orders.

Workers at Ferguson Marine have been invited to apply for voluntary redundancy as construction draws to a close on the second of two long-delayed CalMac ferries.

The Port Glasgow firm currently employs 247 core staff, 31 agency staff and 32 apprentices - but says it expects to shed 70 posts through a voluntary redundancy process.

The Scottish government has promised to directly award the yard new orders for four smaller ships, but ministers say they are still conducting "due diligence" on the plan.

Ferguson Marine said the job losses would protect the long-term viability of the yard - but unions described the move as "a betrayal of a blameless workforce".

BBC Scotland News understands those who choose to leave the firm will receive Â£1,000 per completed year of service, up to Â£10,000, on top of their statutory entitlements.

News.title: One dead and hundreds ill in UK salmonella outbreak
News.content:
Symptoms include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever. These usually develop between 12 and 72 hours after becoming infected.

Anyone who is concerned should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance, says the UKHSA.

Most cases - 199 of the 207 - have been in England, including 47 in London and 38 in Yorkshire and Humber.

Hannah Charles, lead epidemiologist for gastrointestinal infections at UKHSA, said: "We're working with Food Standards Agency and other public health agencies to investigate a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK."

Salmonella can be found in a number of food sources including raw or under-cooked poultry or meat and eggs.

Preparing and cooking food thoroughly can prevent infection, as well as washing your hands after using the bathroom and before handling food.

Thousands of cases food poisoning happen each year in the UK caused by lots of different strains of salmonella.

It is more unusual to see an outbreak like this linked to one specific stain of the bacterium affecting many people at one time.

The UKHSA says "extensive" epidemiological and food chain investigations are ongoing to identify the source but that egg consumption remains the strongest to date.

Some of the food businesses linked to 24 of the cases use imported eggs.

"At this time there is no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry," says the UKHSA.

Any extra precautions or preventative measures will be implemented if needed, it says. The risk to the general public is low.

Jacquelyn McCormick, Head of Incidents at the Food Standards Agency, said eggs which are thoroughly cooked and handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk.

She advised: "Infants, young children, pregnant people and older adults should only eat runny or raw eggs if they have a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain egg assurance scheme."

People handling eggs, eggshells or egg packaging should wash their hands thoroughly with soap and water, she added.

News.title: Disabled people in England to get 24-hour free bus travel
News.content:
Disabled people in England will be able to travel by bus for free at any time of day from April, the government has announced.

Currently, disabled bus passes are only eligible for use between the hours of 09:30 and 23:00 on weekdays, making it difficult for people to get to work or attend later evening events. They can be used at any time of day at the weekend and on bank holidays.

It is believed about one million people could benefit from the change, which forms part of the government's focus on reducing the cost of living and encouraging people into work.

The disability charity Scope said the move would "remove barriers to everyday life".

According to the government, bus travel is the most popular mode of transport in England and a "lifeline for so many".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was "simply not right that many disabled people cannot travel using their pass during certain times of the day".

He said the government would change that, as he had done previously in his role as mayor of Greater Manchester.

Earlier this year, Burnham removed time-restricted travel for those with disabled passes in Manchester so they could use the city's bus system, known as the Bee Network, at any time of day.

"I'm proud to do it now for the whole country," he added.

Tom Gordon, Liberal Democrat MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough and prominent advocate for the policy, called it a "huge win for the disabled community" and a "culmination of two years of campaigning".

But a Conservative Party spokesman asked the prime minister to "come clean" on how he was going to fund "this growing list of policies".

"This is simply the shuffling around of existing departmental budgets," they added.

News.title: Ex-workers tell of 'chaotic atmosphere' at new £400m prison
News.content:
The UK's newest prison has had a "chaotic atmosphere" in its first 18 months, former workers have told a BBC investigation.

HMP Millsike, in East Yorkshire, was heralded by the government for setting "the standard for the future" when it opened in March 2025 with 1,500 places.

But former workers have described under-staffing, inadequate training and seeing specialist officers called in to deal with serious incidents on numerous occasions.

Mitie, the company that runs the category C prison, said safety was its "highest priority" and it was "operating in line with plans agreed with the Ministry of Justice".

News.title: Gillian Anderson felt 'betrayed' by The Salt Path allegations after appearing in adaptation
News.content:
The Salt Path star Gillian Anderson has said allegations that the memoir was fabricated felt like "a betrayal" after spending time with the couple.

Anderson played Raynor Winn in the film adaptation of the 2018 memoir, which was released in the UK last year.

It tells the story of how Winn and her husband Moth, who was diagnosed with a neurological condition, walked the South West Coast Path after losing their Welsh home.

But an investigation by the Observer suggested some of Winn's claims about the events that had led to the couple losing their home had been misrepresented.

Winn previously described the Observer's article as "highly misleading" and said the couple had been taking legal advice.

The book and its film adaptation depict a couple who decide to walk the 630-mile (1,013km) route after their home was repossessed following a bad business deal.

But the Observer reported that Winn - whose legal name is Sally Walker - and her husband, Moth Winn, had lost their home after she had taken out a loan to repay money she had been accused of stealing from her previous employer, Martin Hemmings, an estate agent and property surveyor from north Wales.

In a statement issued last year, Winn said she stood by the book's description of how they came to lose their house, saying the dispute with the Hemmings did not result in her and her husband losing their home.

News.title: Water supply restored to 7,400 properties in Kent, South East Water says
News.content:
Drinking water supplies have been restored to about 7,600 properties in Kent which have been experiencing no water or low pressure, South East Water (SEW) has said.

More than 8,000 customers were affected by the latest supply disruptions, which SEW said was a result of prolonged hot weather, high demand, pipe bursts, and power issues.

The company said supplies had been restored to properties in Herne Bay, Rough Common and Blean, but urged all customers to use water for "essential" purposes only.

About 400 properties in Benenden, Cranbrook and Rolvenden are continuing to experience low pressure or no water and properties in Herne Bay might experience "intermittent supplies" later, SEW added.

News.title: Stag put down after attacking man in Richmond Park
News.content:
A man in his 60s suffered chest injuries after being attacked by a stag in Richmond Park on Saturday.

Royal Parks said the male deer had approached the man's picnic group looking for food, and had since been put down.

Emergency services were called to the south-west London park at 18:16 BST following reports of a deer attack. The Met said a man was taken to hospital, where his injuries were assessed as neither life-threatening nor life-changing.

The charity which maintains London's royal parks has issued a warning to keep "at least 50 metres (165ft) away" from the animals following what they said was a rise in visitors feeding wild animals.

News.title: Watch: Seven GCSE exams, five months, one determined teenager
News.content:
Secondary school pupil Patrick McCabe, 16, has told BBC Breakfast that the wait for his GCSE results on Thursday is "terrifying".

McCabe has cerebral palsy and completed exams in seven subjects over the course of five months using eye-gaze technology - an achievement celebrated by his friends and teachers at school.

The pupil, who describes himself as "hard-working, resilient and a little bit cheeky," said the process was difficult.

McCabe was inspired to take the exams after seeing the late Rob Burrow appear on CBeebies' Bedtime Stories, where he read aloud using an eye-controlled computer.

BBC Breakfast's Jayne McCubbin spoke to Patrick ahead of results day.

Acclaimed film, TV and stage actor Phyllida Law, whose daughters are actors Emma and Sophie Thompson, has died, aged 94.

The news was confirmed by her manager, Jacky Leggo, who said the star “died supremely peacefully at home, surrounded by all of her family”.

Law’s acting career began in 1932, when she won a place at Bristol Old Vic Theatre school, where she originally wanted to be a stage designer. After realising she liked performing, in what she described as a “happy mistake”, Law racked up many roles in Bristol Old Vic plays, where she met her future husband, Eric Thompson.

The pair married in 1957 and remained together until Eric’s death from a heart attack, aged 53, in 1982.

It was stage roles opposite Alec Guinness in John Mortimer’s A Voyage Round My Father at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in 1971, and Alan Bennett’s Habeas Corpus at the Oxford Playhouse in 1973 that established Law as a major stage performer in the 1960s.

Her film credits started in the 1980s, and in the 1990s, Law regularly appeared on-screen opposite her daughters Emma and Sophie. These projects included Peter’s Friends (1992), which was directed by Emma’s then-husband, Kenneth Branagh, as well as Branagh’s version of Much Ado About Nothing (1993), also starring Emma.

In 1997, she appeared once again alongside Emma in Alan Rickman’s directorial debut The Winter Guest, with the pair playing a mother and a daughter.

open image in gallery Phyllida Law with daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson ( Getty )

Law also appeared as Mrs Bates Emma, the 1996 Jane Austen adaptation starring Gwyneth Paltrow, in which Sophie played her daughter. She received an OBE for services to drama and charitable causes in 2014.

More to follow

In recent years, Oslo’s Øya Festival has faced opprobrium. Since 2024, its parent company Superstruct Entertainment has been receiving investment from private equity firm KKR, which also holds some unrelated investments in Israeli companies. In a country that prides itself on humanitarianism – in which corruption and scandal are vanishingly rare – this was a fairly sustained controversy that peaked last summer, with calls to boycott the festival. This year the mood has cooled somewhat, Oya having partnered up with Amnesty, and the wealthy petro-state’s citizens seem content to fly Palestine flags.

For a festival often punctuated by storms, it’s apt that the line-up is stuffed full of moody, dramatic acts. On Wednesday night, The Cure, those emperors of goth and pop, headline the main stage. The Crawley group have an incomparable catalogue of hits to play with, and deliver a sprawling set that even sees Robert Smith shed a tear during a captivating rendition of “Just Like Heaven”. Their set lasts two-and-a-half hours and spans more than four decades, including their early post-punk era, a stint as funereal doomsayers, and the synth-pop of their commercial peak. They save most of the bangers for the 10-song encore: “Lovesong”, “Lullaby”, “The Lovecats”, “Friday I’m in Love” and “Boys Don’t Cry” all ensue. Eschewing tight jeans these days for roomy combat trousers, Smith is leaning into his late sixties, but what remains constant is that voice: crystalline and pained and cracked only when he allows it. Seldom have I seen him more joyous.

Come Thursday evening, it is Nick Cave’s doom-laden sermons that bellow out across the fields, sending the normally polite crowd into a state of bedlam. Opener “Get Ready for Love“ gives way to a career-spanning set that veers from the chaotic, strangled guitar of “From Her to Eternity” to “The Mercy Seat”. Alongside music steeped in biblical imagery, rainfall feels like an accompaniment – as if this besuited preacher had summoned the heavens himself. “Eighty per cent of my songs are about the rain,” he says, having marched through “O Children” and “Train Long-Suffering”, with Warren Ellis pogoing across the stage, violin perched under his chin. By turns apocalyptic and poignant, flowing as it is with meditations on grief, the set ends on “Into My Arms”, a song that targets the tear ducts with laser-guided precision.

On the Circus stage, in a frustrating partial clash with Cave, Dev Hynes aka Blood Orange commands the space with the band’s nocturnal tangle of Prince-adjacent funk, saxophone and bruised falsetto. A Norwegian warehouse is an incongruous setting for songs that feel more at home in the latter hours of a clammy afters, but somehow the music blooms. There’s a soporific quality – on tracks such as the sublime “You’re Not Good Enough” and “Charcoal Baby” – with synths gliding over honeyed vocals. The immaculate coda of “Uncle ACE” drifts over the crowd. Hynes flits between guitar and keys with diffident grace. Melancholy, sensual and unexpectedly communal, this set whispers seductively.

Earlier in the day, Jalen Ngonda goes down a storm. Channelling Jackson Five through Sam Cooke into Otis Redding and Marvin Gaye, the Liverpool-based US singer is a proper throwback. Even his outfit – a purple jacquard jacket with metallic gold geometric threading, and sharp red undershirt bleeding through at collar and cuff – is from another time. And what a voice he has, somersaulting effortlessly through the octaves: rasp one moment, creamy melisma the next.

Later on, festivalgoers flock to Geese, a sprawling post-punk outfit massive right now after the release of their debut album Getting Killed. Theirs is a ramshackle din lent ballast by surreal, acerbic lyrics and frontman Cameron Winter’s vocals, which move between velvety croons and strained shrieks.

A more dulcet counterpoint is provided by Hannah Storm, an exceptionally talented Norwegian singer whose atmospheric piano melodies and retro-pop sensibilities, underpinned by an exquisite and versatile voice, have established her as a commanding presence in her native country.

Girl Group, another home-grown stand-out, arrive on Saturday. Four Norwegians and a Yorkshire musician who met in Liverpool, they dissect the reality of being a woman in 2026 with astuteness and sardonic humour, taking in, among other things, boozy nights out and sexual taboos. Towards the end of their set, they passionately urge Øya to end affiliations with Pepsi and KKR.

open image in gallery Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds perform at Øya festival in Oslo, 2026 ( Raphael Pour-Hashemi )

After a characteristically flamboyant and galvanising performance from Irish powerhouse CMAT, Lily Allen effectively turns the festival stage into a theatre. Playing her recent album, West End Girl in full, Allen arrives in a shimmering gold metallic bow-finished dress. The set recreates her former Brooklyn townhouse: a pink-carpeted bedroom with a made bed, a Smeg fridge stocked with all manner of things, and a velvet chaise longue, all of which render the audience voyeurs, privy to the high-profile collapse of her marriage to David Harbour. She sounds great, and her acting is on point too, as she inhabits the domestic mise-en-scène with a tragicomedy that blends tears with dark humour. While UK audiences complained that the 55-minute runtime and lack of crowd interaction didn’t justify the cost, at a festival, in a field no less, such a novel performance is extra bang for your buck.

Headlining Saturday is Tromsø-born Dagny Sandvik, who stomps her way through a show warmed up by pyrotechnics and pulsing tunes, moving a swooning crowd. I watch for 30 minutes before heading to Underworld, those electronic experimentalists who’ve spent decades pushing the boundaries of sound into territories both dancey and introspective. Everyone’s arms are aloft as they close with “Born Slippy”, with its hammering kick drum, distorted vocals and iconic refrain of “lager, lager, lager”. A sonic shot of adrenaline, it’s the perfect ending to the festival.

Earl Charles Spencer is set to give his perspective on his sister Princess Diana’s life in a revealing new book, ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death.

Diana, Princess of Wales, died aged 36 in August 1997, when a car she was travelling in crashed in Paris’s Pont de l’Alma tunnel. Her funeral was estimated to have been watched by more than two billion people around the world.

Spencer’s book, titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, will mark the first time that he has “spoken openly and at length” about his older sister, according to publisher Penguin Michael Joseph. The British peer is set to tell “the astonishing story of his life with Diana and the tragic week of her death”.

According to Daniel Bunyard, publishing director at Penguin Random House UK, the book will feature “many revelations that will draw considerable attention” but would also offer readers “for the first time, but also for all time, a fitting tribute to the beloved woman who was Princess Diana”.

He added that the book would be one of “historic importance” as well as “utterly unique in being written by Earl Spencer, from a vantage point of such intimacy”.

Earl Spencer said he had decided to write the book because, “with the 30th anniversary of Diana's tragic death on the skyline, I've been inundated yet again with requests for interviews about my sister”.

open image in gallery Charles Spencer ( Getty )

“This has convinced me to write down my own thoughts and memories, once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths that have become accepted over time.”

He added that he’s hoping to “tell the truth about Diana” from his perspective, “just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral”.

The now-62-year-old delivered a eulogy at Diana’s funeral in September 1997, in which he described his sister as “the most hunted person of the modern age” and promised to protect her sons, Princes William and Harry.

“As with my eulogy, I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way,” Spencer continued regarding his book.

“I would be delighted if those too young to remember her in her heyday feel – after reading this – that they ‘get’ who she really was: a one-off, dynamic character, full of love, charisma and self-doubt, who gave life a hell of a go, and left the world a far better place, despite exiting the stage while still so young.”

open image in gallery 'Swan Song: Diana, My Sister' by Charles Spencer ( Penguin )

The book is set to be released on 22 September this year and will be translated into 12 languages.

Spencer has written 10 books about the his family, the royals and his life – one of the most recent being his 2024 memoir A Very Private School. In the book, he revealed that he was sexually abused as a child by a female staff member while at boarding school, which has left him with lifelong “demons”.

French authorities rescued 96 migrants after an inflatable dinghy suffered engine failure in the English Channel on Monday morning, shortly after departing the French coast.

Emergency crews reported that roughly 30 individuals were left in the sea off Le Touquet beach, with several encountering severe difficulties in strong currents. Four people were winched to safety by a helicopter crew, while a lifeboat recovered six others, before the group was taken to the port of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

Elsewhere on Monday, individuals from another craft were photographed by the Press Association arriving at the Border Security Command site in Dover, Kent.

According to Home Office statistics, 250 people completed the crossing across three separate boats during the day.

The operation follows a trend in recent weeks where human trafficking gangs appear to be crowding higher numbers of people onto single vessels, including a record 230 individuals on one boat earlier this month.

open image in gallery Burnham has vowed to take a different approach to tackle smuggling gangs ( AFP/Getty )

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to "change tactics" to counter these smuggling networks.

News of this latest rescue mission comes just days after around 140 migrants attempting to cross the English Channel to the UK were picked up by a French maritime rescue operation in the early hours of Saturday morning.

The complex operation, which deployed a number of rescue boats, began on Friday morning when the monitoring station in Saint-Aubin-sur-Mer spotted a migrant boat heading towards Dieppe, a fishing port on the Normandy coast.

Two patrol boats were then used to track the vessel as it made its way up to the Pas de Calais, the French authorities said on Saturday.

Around 40 people were waiting in the water off the coast near Berck-sur-Mer for the “taxi-boat” late on Friday.

Lifeboats monitored them, fearing they would be stranded by the tide, the maritime prefecture explained. And when they did become stranded, they were taken to the beach to be met by the fire and rescue service.

The boat then resumed its northward journey at around 1am, and reached another beach where 82 people were wearing life-jackets waiting to board.

At this time, there were around 20 people already on board the small boat, the prefecture said. Those waiting for the dinghy decided against boarding due to bad weather, and were again met by French rescuers back on land.

Eventually, those on board abandoned their attempt to cross at around 3.30am.

Fears of fresh conflict in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region are growing as the health system struggles to recover from a devastating civil war that ravaged the region, and as attacks on hospitals and clinics continue.

Healthcare facilities were among the casualties of the 2020-2022 conflict, with health workers killed and abducted, as well as premises looted, occupied and destroyed. The war is estimated to have killed 600,000 people, with systematic looting and widespread destruction resulted in the near-total collapse of one of Ethiopia’s best-performing regional health systems.

The rise in global conflict over the last few years, as well as a change in how wars are fought due to improvements in long-range weapons and drones, has led to an unprecedented surge in attacks on healthcare.

The same is true in Ethiopia and Tigray, with attacks on hospitals and clinics having continued since the war ended.

Healthcare workers were reportedly arrested in July under a new regional proclamation punishing alleged dissent, while in neighbouring region of Amhara, healthcare facilities and ambulances have also been destroyed in government drone strikes in recent months.

Tigray borders Amhara to the south and Afar to the east, both of which were drawn into the war when fighting spread beyond Tigray in 2021.

Health workers have also been abducted and killed this year, the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa (OJAH) group found in a new report.

Attacks on ambulances, looting and armed takeovers of health facilities have been reported across the Afar, Amhara and Tigray regions, while health workers have also been targeted and subjected to violence because of their work, according a new report by Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) and the OJAH. They collected evidence in 2024, 2025 and 2026.

Despite the scale of the attacks on healthcare in Tigray, some of which could potentially constitute war crimes under international law, PHR and OJAH warned there has been little accountability, allowing “widespread impunity”.

“Neither the Ethiopian government nor the international community has prioritised investigation and justice,” their statement said, adding that transitional justice in Ethiopia “has failed to address these harms”.

The Ethiopian government and Tigray authorities have repeatedly denied any breaches of international law.

However, medical staff have reported being targeted and experiencing violence because of their work, continuing a pattern of attacks that could have severe consequences for a health system that has barely recovered from the previous conflict.

In a joint statement, PHR and OJAH warned of a possible collapse, and called on the the Ethiopian government and the international community to ensure protection of health facilities and health care workers.

In March, the Tigray Regional Health Bureau also warned of potential operational collapse, citing chronic shortages of medicines, medical supplies and fuel, as well as health workers who had gone without pay since the beginning of the year.

Forces from the Ethiopian federal army and Tigray have been amassing on either side of the region’s border for the last few months as animosity grows between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the region’s authorities.

Both sides have accused the other of attempting to start a fresh conflict, with clashes near the border with Sudan displacing residents and triggering fears of a return to civil war.

The new OJAH report alleges that United Nations agencies have not follow up either, due to lapsed investigative mechanisms on Ethiopia and gaps in the publishing of data. The UN and its officials have repeatedly called for a deescalation of tensions given the already-dire humanitarian situation in Tigray.

“Accountability is essential to preventing further violence and breaking this cycle of impunity,” Lindsey Green, deputy director of research at PHR, told The Independent. “We cannot look away. Conflict-affected communities across northern Ethiopia deserve unimpeded access to health care, a renewed commitment to rebuilding, and peace, not more violence.”

This year, in May, marked ten years since a United Nations Security Council resolution to condemn acts of violence against health facilities, patients and health workers was unanimously adopted. It renewed a commitment to protect health in conflict, something rooted in international humanitarian law since the first Geneva Convention in 1864.

Ms Green added that communities have already endured violence on a staggering scale, including extreme acts of sexual violence, displacement and the destruction of vital services including healthcare.

The crisis has been compounded by cuts to international aid, with the loss of $380 million (£281m) in foreign assistance in 2025 disrupting medical supplies and services. It has also seen support for survivors of conflict-related sexual violence, food programmes and other health services cut.

The Trump administration is delaying loan forgiveness for some borrowers as it rolls back Biden-era payment credits, a report from Politico has revealed.

For every lost payment credit, borrowers have to wait a month longer for loan forgiveness.

“The past five years have been a series of disappointments for federal student loan borrowers,” Jay Fleischman, a student loan specialist and managing attorney at MoneyWise Law, told The Independent.

The credit rollbacks impact participants in the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program. Borrowers get loan forgiveness for working 10 years in certain public service occupations, such as law enforcement or librarianship, while making 120 qualifying student loan payments.

In 2024, the Biden administration granted payment credits to public service borrowers because of payment-related missteps by certain loan servicers.

open image in gallery Some federal student loan borrowers in the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program have lost payment credits they received from the Biden administration, which means they’ll have to wait even longer for loan forgiveness ( Getty )

The Trump administration decided to annul some of those payment credits that it claims were awarded by the Biden administration in error.

“These errors resulted in inaccurate payment counts for some borrowers,” Department of Education Spokesperson Ellen Keast told The Independent in an email Monday. “The Department remains committed to ensuring that every qualifying payment is properly credited to a borrower’s account.”

Taking away Biden-era payment credits would betray the trust of students who believed the government-granted credits were permanent, Fleishman said in an email to The Independent.

“Though it's important for payment counts to be correct, federal student loan borrowers have made financial and career plans based on the information they've already been provided,” he said. “The administration's actions threaten to derail the progress millions have made toward loan forgiveness.”

Borrowers have faced massive changes to the federal student loan system over the past five years.

In 2023, the Biden administration added the income-driven SAVE plan to the list of repayment choices for borrowers. The plan limited borrower payments to 5 percent of their discretionary income and provided loan forgiveness after 20 to 25 years.

A federal judge declared the plan unconstitutional and ordered the government to end the SAVE Plan in March 2026.

open image in gallery Department of Education Secretary Linda McMahon has led efforts to overhaul federal student loan repayment plans and roll back erroneous Biden-era payment credits. ‘Though it's important for payment counts to be correct, federal student loan borrowers have made financial and career plans based on the information they've already been provided,’ a department spokesperson said ( AFP/Getty )

Some 7.5 million borrowers were forced to choose a new plan because their SAVE Plan no longer existed. Starting July 1, borrowers received notices that they had 90 days to choose a replacement plan.

In the meantime, the Trump administration chose to end one other income-driven repayment plan by 2028 - PAYE. It introduced the RAP (Repayment Assistance Plan) as a replacement for all other income-driven plans.

Borrowers who lost their SAVE Plan will receive a notice to pick a new plan by the end of the year, according to the education department.

News.content:

A Trump administration task force created to combat antisemitism pushed for settlements with Ivy League universities despite government investigations that were rushed and incomplete or that failed to establish legal violations by the schools, a former Justice Department lawyer alleged in a whistleblower disclosure obtained by The Associated Press.

The complaint alleges that the investigations into some of the nation's most prestigious academic institutions were designed to strong-arm the schools into cutting deals for political purposes. Outcomes of the investigations were "predetermined, without regard to the evidence" in a “politically mandated effort” to extract money from schools through settlement demands and funding freezes under the pretext of rooting out antisemitism, the complaint alleges.

The work of the multi-agency task force, launched by the Justice Department under then-Attorney General Pam Bondi in February 2025, was “marked by extraordinary procedural irregularities, predetermined outcomes without factual or legal support” and disregard for the law and Constitution, lawyers for the former government attorney wrote in seeking watchdog investigations into their client's complaints.

The complaint taps into a broader public discussion about the administration's efforts to confront allegations of antisemitism at colleges, a problem that received renewed attention during campus protests over Israel's war in Gaza that some Jewish students said made them feel unsafe. President Donald Trump returned to the White House with a goal of rooting out antisemitism that he said had gone unchecked during the Biden administration, but critics have called his government's response heavy-handed and said it infringed on free speech rights and coerced concessions from public institutions.

A key House Democrat is publicizing the whistleblower's allegations

Lawyers for the former Justice Department attorney, identified as Haley Van Erem, filed the disclosure Tuesday with the inspectors general at the departments of Justice and Health and Human Services and the Office of Special Counsel.

Van Erem spent nearly a decade working in the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division before being assigned to help with the task force last year.

She left the Justice Department in May 2025 because she was "unwilling to be made vulnerable to further participation in politically motivated investigations unsupported by facts and contrary to law," according to the complaint, which also accuses the task force of having targeted Muslim professors.

Spokespeople for the Justice Department and Health and Human Services Department did not immediately respond to requests seeking comment Tuesday.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, wrote separately to Harmeet Dhillon, who as the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has been a public face of the department's efforts to counter antisemitism. In his letter, he said antisemitism at colleges and medical schools is a real problem that needs to be investigated.

“But,” he told Dhillon, “your 'investigation’ into antisemitism was fake, a pre-baked frame-up operation thoroughly political in nature.”

Raskin wrote that “the whole project was designed to harass professors and administrators at major universities, to curtail their freedom of speech and academic freedom, and to strip targeted institutions of hundreds of millions of dollars in grants that they had already been awarded on the merits of their applications.”

Scrutiny over the handling of investigations into elite schools

The whistleblower complaint deals chiefly with investigations into three Ivy League universities: Brown, Harvard and Columbia.

It alleges that in the case of Brown, the investigative team did not find evidence to support a violation of Title VI, the section of the Civil Rights Act that bars discrimination on the basis of race, color or national origin in programs that receive federal funding, but that “leadership refused to permit a notice of no violation and instead sought some form of settlement or resolution despite acknowledging the absence of a legal basis for doing so.”

Investigators did find evidence of discrimination at Columbia, the complaint says, but the investigation was done on an accelerated timetable before adequate factual development and legal review were completed and relied on allegations that “were unsupported, based on news reports or litigation filings, or that implicated protected First Amendment activity."

Columbia University agreed to pay the government $200 million as part of an agreement restoring access to federal funding. Brown University separately agreed to pay $50 million to Rhode Island workforce development organizations to end the three federal investigations involving allegations of antisemitism and racial bias in admissions, with no findings of wrongdoing.

In the investigation into Harvard, Trump administration officials discussed “extraordinary funding freezes and sweeping proposed settlement terms” before an investigation had been completed that could establish Title VI violations. Sean Keveney, then-HHS acting general counsel, said he believed Harvard would settle because they were “over a barrel,” according to the complaint.

A federal judge last year ordered the Trump administration to reverse its cuts of more than $2.6 billion in research funding for the university, saying the government “used antisemitism as a smokescreen for a targeted, ideologically-motivated assault on this country’s premier universities.” And a different judge last week dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit that accused Harvard University of turning a blind eye to harassment of Jewish students.

Madonna leads the 2026 MTV Video Music Award nominations, the network announced Tuesday.

The pop superstar has been nominated in every decade of her musical career. She has 19 competitive MTV VMA wins and in 1986 became the first solo female artist to receive the Video Vanguard Award.

She is up for 11 awards at this year's ceremony, including video, artist and song of the year as well as best collaboration, dance, direction, art direction, cinematography, editing, choreography and visual effects.

If she were to sweep, she'd tie Beyoncé and Taylor Swift for the title of most-awarded musician in VMA history. They have 30 each. (Eminem is the male artist with the most VMAs, with 15.)

Speaking of Swift: She follows Madonna with the second-most nominations, with nine. If she takes home even one award, she will become the most-awarded artist in VMA history.

Swift is up for video and artist of the year as well as best pop, direction, art direction, cinematography, editing, choreography and visual effects.

Madonna and Swift are followed by Ariana Grande and Sabrina Carpenter with seven nods to their name as well as Bruno Mars, PinkPantheress and Zara Larsson with five. Blackpink's LISA has four and Shakira, Tate McRae, GENER8ION and Yung Lean are tied for three.

Rounding out the artist of the year category nominees are Grande, Mars, Carpenter and Morgan Wallen, in addition to Madonna and Swift.

The top prize of the night, video of the year, sees Swift's “The Fate of Ophelia” compete against Madonna’s “Confessions II — The Film,” Grande’s “Hate That I Made You Love Me,” Mars' “I Just Might,” Carpenter’s “Tear” and GENER8ION’s “Storm” starring Yung Lean.

The two-hour show will broadcast live on CBS on Sunday, Sept. 27, at 7:30 p.m. Eastern and 4:30 p.m. Pacific, from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. It will also simulcast on MTV and be available to stream on Paramount+ in the U.S.

The show will become available to stream globally the next day on Paramount+ and MTV.

CBS is home to a number of award shows, including the Tony Awards and the American Music Awards. It has aired the Grammys since 1973, though that show will head to ABC in 2027.

This year’s Video Music Awards features 26 first-time nominees, which include GENER8ION and Yung Lean (with their aforementioned three nods, for their “Storm” collaboration) and the K-pop boy band CORTIS and viral “Boston” singer Stella Lefty with two each. Other notable first-time nominees include Don Toliver, Kali Uchis, Noah Kahan, Olivia Dean, Tucker Wetmore and Sienna Spiro.

The best dance category has returned for the first time in seven years. Nominees include McRae's “Nobody’s Girl,” Bebe Rexha and Faithless' “New Religion,” Harry Styles' “Aperture,” Lady Gaga and Doechii's “Runaway,” Madonna's “Confessions II — The Film,” PinkPantheress' “Stateside” with Larsson and Slayyyter's “Dance …”

Fan voting began online Tuesday across 13 categories and ends Sept. 25 at 6 p.m. Eastern and 3 p.m. Pacific.

Voting in the best new artist category will remain active during the show.

News.title: Unemployment rate fails to fall for Burnham
News.content:
An expected drop in the unemployment rate has failed to materialise, dealing a setback to Andy Burnham’s hopes of reviving Britain’s ailing economy.

Unemployment remained stuck at 4.9pc in the three months to June, while the number of payrolled employees fell by 13,000, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics. Economists had predicted that the unemployment rate would ease to 4.8pc.

While the three-month figure was flat, monthly data showed a sharp increase at the end of the period. Unemployment jumped to 5.4pc in June, up from 4.6pc the previous month.

That marked the highest reading since October 2020 and the biggest monthly jump in 13 years.

Julian Jessop, at the Institute of Economic Affairs, described the latest jobs figures as “dire”.

He said: “The unemployment rate remains stubbornly high, with a big jump in the single month figure for June.”

It came as private sector wage growth slumped to a six-year low of just 2.8pc. That stands in contrast to a 6.1pc pay increase for the average public sector worker in the same period.

Meanwhile, vacancies dropped to 707,000 in the three months to July – the lowest level since 2021 – with a particular strain on entry-level job openings.

Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, warned that the UK was “trapped in a deepening jobs drought”.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “Stagnant, or even negative, real wage growth in the second half of this year will intensify the pressure on Burnham and Healey to come up with a package to support the cost of living.

“However, doing anything substantial without breaching either the fiscal rules or the manifesto commitments looks increasingly difficult given the deterioration in headroom and commitments to spend big on everything from defence to social care.”

News.title: Top British scientist steps down from WHO
News.content:
One of Britain’s best-known scientists has resigned as assistant director-general of the World Health Organization.

Sir Jeremy Farrar became a household name during the pandemic when he served on the UK’s Scientific Advisory Group for Emergencies (Sage).

Sources inside the WHO and the broader scientific community told The Telegraph he resigned his position on Monday.

While it is not clear what prompted his resignation, colleagues told The Telegraph he had been unhappy within the organisation for some time. One speculated that he had become increasingly frustrated with its internal politics and bureaucracy.

Sir Jeremy, 64, who was also a former director of the Wellcome Trust, could not immediately be reached for comment.

The surprise move comes at a difficult time for the WHO, which is undergoing a major restructuring after suffering cuts and a massive funding shortfall following the United States’s withdrawal from it in January. It is also fighting a major outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s Director-General, announced Dr Farrar’s decision in an email to all staff on Tuesday morning, saying that the British scientist will “retire” from the WHO, effective September 30.

In the email, seen by The Telegraph, Dr Tedros said: “Dr Farrar has demonstrated an exceptional commitment to science and public health at the highest levels, and we are grateful that he chose to bring his experience, energy and conviction to WHO.

“On behalf of the entire organisation, I extend my sincere thanks to Dr Farrar... [and wish] him every success in his next chapter and a well-deserved retirement.”

He added that Dr Bruce Aylward will take over as the new Assistant Director-General for Health Promotion, Disease Prevention and Care.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football: five key budget enablers
News.content:
As the new Telegraph Fantasy Football season approaches, the fantasy football experts at Fantasy Football Hub will continue to bring you the very best in fantasy football knowledge, tips and tools to help you rise up the ranks and win your mini-leagues.

To join the Hub and get access to all their great resources and expert tips you can take advantage of its 50% pre-season discount here.

Telegraph Fantasy Football managers need to make compromises to fit in fantasy heavyweights like Erling Haaland (£8.3m) and Bruno Fernandes (6.5m). Picking some set-and-forget budget enablers who have either high point ceiling potential or will return a steady stream of points, is key to freeing up those funds.

Below are five players the Fantasy Football Hub experts have highlighted for consideration.





Brian Brobbey (£3.3m)

The Sunderland forward had a steady Premier League debut season, netting seven times and helping the Black Cats qualify for the Europa League. The Dutch international netted three times at the World Cup, improving his stock further, and will be looking to get off to a goal-scoring start against Ipswich and Fulham in GWs 1 and 2.



Enzo Le Fee (£3.3m)

Depending on the formation TFF managers are using, Brobbey’s midfield teammate at the same price may be the preferred route to target those opening fixtures. The 26-year-old accrued 12 attacking returns last season, and bumped up his overall score with an impressive 93 tackles.



Harry Wilson (£3.2m)

The midfielder swapped London for Yorkshire in the summer, as he looks to expand on a whopping 17 attacking returns from last season. Feeding the rejuvenated Dominic Calvert-Lewin (£3.9m), and adding goals from midfield for Leeds will be two primary objectives for the Welsh international, who could make a mockery of his mere marginal price increase.



James Trafford (£3.0m)

Another Leeds United summer acquisition, Daniel Farke fought off rival Premier League suitors to land the ex-Manchester City shot-stopper. Leeds United have a mixed bag in terms of opening fixture difficulty, but do have three home league games in the first five before the international break, and the new no.1 has an outside chance of getting the nod in the Carabao Cup games too, so there are points available should the Whites be able to shut out the opposition.



James Hill (£2.6m)

If looking to fit in more big-hitters, a sub £3m player can be extremely useful for team balance, and the Bournemouth defender looks assured of starting having played a pivotal role in getting the Cherries into Europe this season.
